enrichment.short_title: Planning approval quashed where council failed to consider its own safety objections in reserved matters decision
key_facts: Tendring District Council refused planning permission in February 2003 for 77 dwellings at Parkeston near a Carless refinery within HSE consultation distance, citing safety/evacuation and highway environmental capacity concerns.

After a confidential report summarising counsel's advice on costs risk, a differently composed committee approved reserved matters and full permission in June 2003 without adequately addressing those objections in the public report.
An inspector later dismissed the developer's appeal on safety grounds; local residents challenged the June approvals by judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of two linked planning decisions: approval of reserved matters for 77 dwellings and grant of full permission for ancillary parking and pumping station.
enrichment.outcome: Both June 2003 approvals quashed; defendant ordered to pay claimant's costs on the standard basis subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority's own earlier reasons for refusing development remain material when determining reserved matters where outline permission did not cap dwelling numbers; it is procedurally unfair and misleading to omit those objections from the public committee report and address their merits only in closed session via counsel's advice.
legal_issues: Whether February refusal grounds were material to June reserved matters applications
Whether the authority could control dwelling numbers at the reserved matters stage under a bare outline permission

enrichment.short_title: Professional litigation funder MPC not liable for defendants' costs after failed Arkin competition claim
key_facts: Managers and Processors of Claims (MPC) funded expert and disbursement costs for impecunious claimant Mr Arkin's large commercial competition claim under a contingent fee agreement taking 25%/23% of recoveries.

MPC's agreement gave conduct of proceedings to Arkin and leading counsel, with MPC unable to control litigation strategy or settlement without counsel's overriding decision.

enrichment.outcome: Application refused; court declined to exercise discretion to order MPC to pay defendants' costs.

Balance between access to justice, deterrence of weak claims, and protection of due administration of justice
Effect of contingent profit share and lack of ATE insurance
Distinction between pure funders and professional funders

enrichment.short_title: Pub owner may be prosecuted under Food Safety Act for selling under-strength spirits, not only licensee
key_facts: Trading standards officers tested whisky and gin bottles at the Slug and Fiddle, Nottingham, finding alcohol content below permitted tolerances.
Nottingham City Council prosecuted brewery owner Wolverhampton and Dudley Breweries; the magistrates held only the licensee could be liable for selling alcohol.
The owner employed the licensee and owned the stock and premises; no test purchases were made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from Nottingham Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court on a point of law under section 14 Food Safety Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; question answered that the owner may be prosecuted; case remitted; certified question of general public importance; leave to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 14 Food Safety Act 1990 should bear its ordinary meaning for all food including alcoholic drink; licensing-law restrictions on who may sell intoxicating liquor do not immunise the pre-sale owner who authorises the sale from food-safety prosecution, and Goodfellow v Johnson is not binding where based on a misreading of Hotchin v Hindmarsh.
legal_issues: Whether only a licensee or servant can 'sell' alcohol for section 14 purposes
Interaction between Food Safety Act 1990 and licensing legislation
Whether Goodfellow v Johnson precludes prosecution of the brewery owner
Whether sampling by trading standards constituted a deemed sale

enrichment.short_title: CPS ordered to pay costs after losing dispute over matrimonial home proceeds subject to confiscation
key_facts: Mrs Grimes claimed a 50% beneficial interest in net proceeds of sale of the matrimonial home held on a joint deposit account after a Crown Court confiscation order against her ex-husband for counterfeiting.

The CPS had made no settlement offer and largely ignored correspondence asserting Mrs Grimes' claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal by Mrs Grimes against the no-order-as-to-costs decision in concurrent Administrative Court and Family Division proceedings between the CPS and an intervener.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; CPS ordered to pay Mrs Grimes' costs before Wilson J, subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: The CPS litigates as an ordinary party for costs purposes; where it loses after a contested hearing and made no offer to settle, CPR 44.3 requires costs to follow the event unless specific factors justify departure—the judge erred by starting from the CPS's special public status rather than the general rule.
legal_issues: Whether the CPS enjoys special immunity from the usual costs-follow-the-event rule
Proper application of CPR 44.3 in confiscation-related interpleader proceedings
Whether Mrs Grimes acted unreasonably in litigating without full documentary proof

enrichment.short_title: VAT section 73(2) assessment must relate to period of original credit, not disclosure period
key_facts: Laura Ashley accounted for VAT on full retail prices for interest-free credit sales; after Primback it claimed repayments for overpaid output tax from October 1996 to July 1999.
Credits for October 1996 and October 1997 repayment periods were paid in March 2000 following voluntary disclosure.
Customs issued a section 73(2) assessment in October 2000 for the October 1999 period (when disclosure was received) to recover those credits if Primback was reversed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision favouring the taxpayer on the validity of a section 73(2) assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Commissioners' appeal dismissed; assessment for October 1999 period held invalid as made for wrong accounting periods.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 73(2) VATA 1994 the prescribed accounting period is that to which the wrongly paid VAT credit relates—here the original over-declaration periods—not the period in which a voluntary disclosure is made; Croydon Hotels is distinguishable where credit could only be claimed in a later return.
legal_issues: Which prescribed accounting period triggers section 73(2) assessment time limits
Construction of 'paid or credited' in section 73(2)
Application of Croydon Hotel and Leisure Co Ltd
Practical consequences for delayed repayment claims

enrichment.short_title: Robbery conviction quashed after West Midlands Serious Crime Squad misconduct affected interview evidence
key_facts: Cummiskey was convicted in 1985 of robbery and firearms offences after a Post Office security van robbery in Coventry; co-defendant Meads' conviction was later quashed due to Serious Crime Squad misconduct.

enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe; defendant's costs order made; no retrial ordered given elapsed time and completed sentence.

legal_issues: Whether West Midlands Serious Crime Squad disclosure rendered the conviction unsafe
Impact of abandoning interview evidence on remaining scientific and identification evidence
Application of the Pendleton test for fresh evidence on appeal

key_facts: Newham granted the Chowdhurys an introductory tenancy in October 2001; housing benefit applications were incomplete and initially refused, causing substantial rent arrears.

key_facts: Virgin Retail held a 25-year lease of a large Liverpool shopping-centre unit (~21,000 sq ft) with upwards-only rent review requiring overall per sq ft valuation and excluding zoning comparables under 5,000 sq ft.
